articles.title: The Senate races that will define the Democratic Party
articles.summary: Primaries have trended progressive, and whether that proves to be a winning formula at the statewide level will be among the defining questions of this cycle.
articles.body:
Now that primary season has nearly come to a close, the Democratic Party has a better sense of where things stand ahead of the general election, and, in most cases, the next few months ought to be a highly competitive sprint to November’s finish line.

Indeed, a number of key Senate races are shaping up to be toss-ups, for better or for worse.

For the better, Democrat Mary Peltola advanced to the general election for Alaska’s highly coveted Senate seat, which both parties agree is crucial to winning control of the upper chamber.

Notably, with 80 percent of votes counted, Peltola is more than 5 points ahead of Republican Dan Sullivan (approximately 48 percent to 43 percent), providing a glimpse of hope for Democrats who believe Peltola is the only Democratic candidate who could pose a true threat to two-term incumbent Sullivan.

Unlike the progressives emerging from primaries in Texas and Minnesota, Peltola has taken a much less partisan approach, distancing herself from former Vice President Kamala Harris specifically and the national Democratic brand generally — a strategy that may prove to be a defining test for how Democrats can compete in a red-leaning terrain.

While her approach has come under fire from her Republican opponent — who has repeatedly emphasized Peltola’s funding from “Lower 48 liberals” — it may do just enough to make inwards with independents and unaffiliated voters tired of partisan politics as usual.

In a Data for Progress general election poll conducted one day before the primary, Peltola led Sullivan by 6 points (53 percent to 47 percent), largely mirroring her winning margin in the actual primary election.

That said, both candidates have significant resources at their disposal, and a 5-point lead in the primary — where other candidates are snagging a few crucial percentage points — isn’t enough for Alaska Democrats to get too comfortable before the general.

Elsewhere, the primaries have trended progressive, and whether that proves to be a winning formula at the statewide level will be among the defining questions of this cycle.

In Texas, Democrat James Talarico is currently neck-and-neck with Republican Ken Paxton, the Trump-endorsed Attorney General who handily defeated incumbent Senator John Cornyn (R-Texas) in May’s Republican runoff.

Despite President Trump’s backing of Paxton in a state he won by nearly 14 points in 2024, Talarico has either led or tied Paxton in all major polling since the runoff, except for the latest Emerson poll , where Paxton leads by 1 point (47 percent to 46 percent).

Even with Talarico’s potential to appeal to independents and Republicans disaffected by Paxton, it is hard to imagine a majority of voters in the Lone Star State electing a progressive Democrat, who had publicly argued that “God is nonbinary” and believes in the complete dismantling of Immigration and Customs Enforcement. A Democratic win in Texas would be a significant upset regardless of who the nominee is, but Talarico’s profile makes that already steep climb steeper still.

Nonetheless, Talarico’s ability to keep up with Paxton is a step in the right direction for the larger party, despite recent internal divisions.

In Minnesota, progressive Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan (D) advanced to the general election after defeating moderate Angie Craig by 20 points earlier this month. Now, Flanagan battles Republican Michele Tafoya for the Senate seat, leading by 5 points (46 percent to 41 percent) in the latest poll conducted since the August 11 primary.

Flanagan’s margin is the least surprising of these progressive primary wins — Minnesota’s electorate has long leaned left, and the state’s charged atmosphere around immigration enforcement has buoyed candidates with strong anti-ICE positions. Still, the race is far from settled.

Michigan Democrats are in a similar boat. Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan’s uber-progressive Democratic nominee for Senate, has a long, uphill battle ahead of November, when he will go head-to-head with uncontested Republican Mike Rogers. El-Sayed won the Democratic primary by 1 point against moderate Rep. Haley Stevens, 47.5 percent to 48.5 percent. He now faces one of the nation’s most contentious races this cycle.

Unlike Texas — where a Democrat winning would be a striking upset regardless of ideology — Michigan is a true purple state. El-Sayed’s general election performance will serve as a referendum on whether the far-left flank is strong enough to win a swing state that’s key to 2028.

Recent polling also indicates quite the toss-up: A Fox News poll has Rogers up by 4 points (51 percent to 47 percent), whereas a Susquehanna poll has El-Sayed ahead by 7 points (46 percent to 39 percent). Other polls have shown El-Sayed up, but by smaller margins.

Taken together, it is clear that the fight to succeed Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.) remains the race to watch. And whether El-Sayed can flip the party on its head and secure a win in a critical swing state will give national Democrats enough to know which way the party should turn ahead of 2028.

Douglas E. Schoen and Carly Cooperman are pollsters and partners with the public opinion company Schoen Cooperman Research based in New York. They are co-authors of the book “ America: Unite or Die. “

articles.title: What does it mean to be Jewish in a time of rising antisemitism?
articles.summary: The state of California is poised to become the first in the nation to recognize being Jewish as an ethnic and racial, not just a religious, identity.
articles.body:
The state of California is poised to become the first in the nation to recognize being Jewish as an ethnic and racial, not just a religious, identity.

On Aug. 13, a key committee of its state Senate passed a bill that would add “Jewish” to its long list of recognized identities. This is an important step forward in a longstanding debate about whether that label denotes just a religion or is an ethnicity or race. As The New York Times observes , it is “a first step toward acknowledging and demystifying the multifaceted nature of Jewish identity.”

But it comes at a dangerous moment for American Jews, a moment of rising antisemitism and anti-Jewish hate crimes.

Critics contend that the bill “could well exacerbate antisemitism.” They draw lessons from history, noting how Nazis and others have denounced Jews for being members of an inferior race . Germany’s Adolf Hitler and the Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin treated Jews as an ethnic group and used that designation as justification for state-sponsored antisemitism.

That is why California, which has the second-largest Jewish population in the U.S. , needs not only to allow the state to recognize them as members of an ethnic or racial group but, as it does so, to redouble its efforts to combat antisemitism in the state and protect its Jewish population.

If the bill passes, the governor and legislature should be ready for it to be weaponized by hate groups. Although Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) has already signed important legislation addressing antisemitism and the rise in hate crimes, new efforts should include increased funding for security at Jewish community centers, schools and houses of worship.

California should also adopt the recommendations contained in the 2023 National Strategy to Counter Antisemitism, including tracking antisemitism online and developing robust information-sharing strategies to help stop violence against Jews before it happens.

And rest assured, the legislation’s impact will not be confined to the Golden State. Jewish leaders and government officials everywhere need to keep their eyes on what is happening in California and be ready to deal with the ripple effects.

Whatever its fate, the bill will not settle the longstanding debate about whether being Jewish is more than a religious designation. An article from the Federation of Jewish Ministries says , “The history of the Jewish people goes back to the early 2nd millennium BCE (over 4,000 years ago). They began as a family. However, as they grew, over the centuries, the Jewish population has experienced diaspora and dispersion, leading to various cultural and ethnic branches.”

Twenty years ago, biologist Alain F. Corcos entered the fray, arguing that because “they never avoided crossbreeding and converted many non-Jews … therefore there is no way to genetically characterize them as a race.”

Even courts in this country have been pulled into the debate about how to categorize Jews. In 1987, the U.S. Supreme Court took up the case of a Jewish congregation in Maryland that sued the perpetrators who had allegedly painted their synagogue with anti-Semitic slogans. They contended that those acts violated federal civil rights laws passed in the wake of the Civil War prohibiting racial discrimination.

A federal magistrate judge in Louisiana put it this way in 2018: “Modern sociologists and anthropologists … debate whether Judaism is a people, a religion, or both. There is no doubt, however, that many people have and continue to view being Jewish as a racial identity.”

A survey conducted by the Pew Research Center confirms that view. “When asked whether being Jewish is mainly a matter of religion, ancestry, culture, or some combination of those things … just one-in-ten [said] it is only a matter of religion.”

In the end, as President Biden wrote in 2023 , antisemitism “undermine[s] our efforts to build a culture of respect … and to our broader vision of a thriving, inclusive, and diverse democracy.” The bill now before the California legislature should be applauded for recognizing that the diversity Biden praises is not just about what happens between groups but also within them.

As California state Sen. Henry Stern (D), the bill’s chief sponsor, told The New York Times, to be a Jew in America requires “being really comfortable with tension … and understanding that we’re a people, we’re a nation, we’re an ethnicity, we are a religion, too.'” His bill reflects just that understanding.

Austin Sarat is the William Nelson Cromwell Professor of Jurisprudence and Political Science at Amherst College.

articles.title: Trump blames New York prosecutors for Cohen’s role in hush money trial
articles.summary: President Trump blamed New York Attorney General Letitia James (D) and Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg (D) for pressuring his former fixer Michael Cohen to testify against him in the 2024 hush money trial. “They threatened you with jail. They threatened you with everything if you didn’t go against Trump,” the president told Cohen in…
articles.body:
President Trump blamed New York Attorney General Letitia James (D) and Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg (D) for pressuring his former fixer Michael Cohen to testify against him in the 2024 hush money trial.

“They threatened you with jail. They threatened you with everything if you didn’t go against Trump,” the president told Cohen in an interview on WABC that aired on Sunday. “And you took it back. I wouldn’t even be talking to you right now if you didn’t, to be honest.”

The ex-attorney testified during the president’s New York hush money criminal trial, and a jury later convicted Trump — who was in the midst of his third presidential campaign — on 34 counts of falsifying business records to keep his alleged affair with adult film actress Stormy Daniels quiet ahead of the 2016 election.

Cohen previously served two-plus years in federal prison after pleading guilty in 2018 to eight criminal counts connected to the payment scheme.

After he was sentenced, the president’s former personal lawyer sued the Trump Organization to cover his financial penalties and legal fees and kicked off a years-long feud with his former client. But in January, Cohen claimed James and Bragg pushed him to testify against Trump in the hush money case.

“Letitia James and Alvin Bragg may not share the same office, but they share the same playbook,” he wrote in a Substack post .

In the radio interview, Trump said the New York officials “used” his former fixer during the criminal trial.

“What you did was actually a brave thing, because you said what they did was wrong,” the president remarked. “You agreed that your testimony, they forced you to say things that you didn’t want to say.”

The president has appealed the conviction , leaning into the Supreme Court’s presidential immunity ruling . The case remains entangled in legal battles.

articles.title: Has questionable MAGA behavior become a new norm?
articles.summary: The ongoing candidacy of individuals like Rep. Max Miller and gubernatorial nominee Victor Marx reflects a shift in American politics toward accepting controversial figures due to Donald Trump’s significant influence over the Republican voter base.
articles.body:
Sometimes you have to do a double take on American politics 2026.

At first glance, a Republican congressman getting support from Republican leaders for reelection is nothing out of the ordinary.

But a second look reveals that Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) has that backing, despite being accused of physically abusing his ex-wife, the daughter of Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio).

His ex-girlfriend, Stephanie Grisham, the former Trump White House press secretary, similarly accused him of abuse and filed for a restraining order .

Most disturbingly, Miller’s ex-wife alleges that he physically abused their two-year-old daughter, including in one instance in which she says he broke the child’s collarbone . Moreno has said Miller is a “danger to his daughter” and that he “holds his breath” every time Miller is around his granddaughter.

Incredibly, Miller still has Republican backing. Neither President Trump, House Speaker Mike Johnson (R- La.) nor the chair of the Republican National Committee, Joe Gruters, have withdrawn their support for Miller.

Here is another reason to do a double taks: The Republican nominee for governor of Colorado, Victor Marx, claims to have killed a person in his youth and refuses to say whether that was the only time he killed someone.

As a Los Angeles Times piece put it : “When Victor Marx was 3 years old, he was forced into a voodoo ritual involving a beheaded cat. At age 7, he killed a man…”

Also, he claims to have rescued 45,000 captives, both children and women, from abuse. He says he “called in a U.S. military airstrike that killed 70 ISIS fighters.” He also claims to have “exorcised demons — and can do so over the telephone, he says, if need be,” according to the Times piece.

Note there is no record of any civilian using American military airpower against Middle Eastern terrorists.

Despite his history and wild claims, Marx remains the Republican nominee for governor of Colorado. He is endorsed by the Republican Governors Association.

In 2012, Republican leaders urged a Missouri congressman, Todd Akin, to get out of a U.S. Senate race after he said that “legitimate rape” rarely results in pregnancy.

Today, Akin’s wild claims would barely register in Trump’s MAGA Republican Party.

Weeks before the 2026 midterms, Miller and Marx remain as candidates in a party led by a president who enforces a low bar for wrongdoing by Republicans, notably himself.

Trump has the support of Republican voters even after a jury found him liable for sexually abusing a woma n and ordered him to pay her more than $5 million.

Trump was also found guilty of hiding a pay-off to a porn star to stop her from talking about a relationship with him.

Indifference to questionable behavior extends to his aides.

Before the August recess, all but two Republican senators voted to confirm Todd Blanche as attorney general. He is the Trump official most responsible for the government’s failure to release all documents tied to the child sex abuse trafficking ring run by Jeffrey Epstein, a former associate of the president.

The “see-no-evil,” reality of Republican politics today is based on Trump’s hold over Republican voters.

They give the president between 80 percent approval, according to YouGov polling .

That support is far above the 35 percent approval given Trump by all voters in a Reuters poll . Nationally, disapproval of his presidency now stands at 57.2 percent, according to the RealClearPolitics average of polls .

All that separates Trump from near zero approval is his base. They stand by him and other Republicans with highly questionable records and statements.

This is the new normal induced by Trump in 2026.

Democrats have pushed two candidates off the ballot who face allegations of mistreating women: Senate candidate Graham Platner in Maine and gubernatorial candidate Eric Swalwell in California.

Trump-style politics holds a different standard.

Trump’s indifference to higher gas prices, for example, requires his base to put loyalty to him above their own economic reality.

Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) recently described the Trump administration as far from a party of the working class but as “a government of, by and for the ultra-rich.”

In fact, two of his Cabinet secretaries, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Education Secretary Linda McMahon, have more wealth than millions of the poorest American households combined.

The Associated Press’ Thomas Beaumont reported last week that “57 Trump [appointed] officials are worth at least $100 million, including 17 ambassadors and the remaining 40 in senior posts across the executive branch.”

Trump’s supporters applaud his populist criticism of out of touch elites. But what about the reality of Trump having the super-rich to run the country.

What about his family increasing its wealth as he is in office.

The Wall Street Journal editorial page recently described Trump’s family as “profiting off the presidency in ways that demean the office.”

Earlier, there was no consequence in Trump’s political world for the fact that he has been found liable for fraud for making false financial statements about his business in New York to get cheaper loans.

If this is the new norm in American politics, it deserves a second look.

Juan Williams is senior political analyst for Fox News Channel and a prize-winning civil rights historian. He is the author of the new book “ New Prize for These Eyes: The Rise of America’s Second Civil Rights Movement . “

articles.title: Arbitrator orders Washington Post to reinstate fired columnist
articles.summary: An independent arbitrator ordered The Washington Post to rehire a columnist it fired last year over controversial social media posts following the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. A judge ruled Karen Attiah, an opinion writer at the Post, had been wrongfully terminated over the social media posts and that the outlet failed to prove…
articles.body:
An independent arbitrator ordered The Washington Post to rehire a columnist it fired last year over controversial social media posts following the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk.

A judge ruled Karen Attiah, an opinion writer at the Post, had been wrongfully terminated over the social media posts and that the outlet failed to prove they amounted to “gross misconduct.”

The Post, the judge ruled, “did not have good and sufficient cause” to terminate Attiah and had violated the news organization’s collective bargaining agreement. As part of the ruling, the company was ordered to reinstate the writer and compensate her with back pay from the time she was fired.

Last fall, after the killing of Kirk, Attiah published a series of online posts in which she suggested she would not mourn the death of Kirk , which the Post argued hurt the company’s reputation and integrity.

“This decision confirms what we’ve said from the start: I was doing my job as an opinion journalist, and doing that job is not misconduct,” Attiah said in a statement issued through her attorney. “After spending over a decade of my career at the Post as an editor and an opinion columnist focusing on race, gender and global human rights, I’m relieved to finally have that record set straight.”

A spokesperson for the company said it respects the arbitration process and declined to comment further.

The Post has gone through an overhaul of its newsroom and opinion section in recent months, as its billionaire owner Jeff Bezos looks to retool its business model.

Some Post readers have canceled their subscriptions and accused Bezos of attempting to shore up relations with President Trump.

articles.title: 25 years after 9/11, Bin Laden has achieved one of his major goals
articles.summary: A Marine veteran argues that twenty-five years of post-9/11 military spending and global counterterrorism efforts have failed to defeat terrorism and instead fulfilled Osama bin Laden’s goal of crippling the American economy.
articles.body:
On Sept. 10, 2001, I got into an argument with one of my friends about our planned day trip to the World Trade Center the next day . He told me he did not want to wake up early. I argued that we should get there as soon as possible, so that we could maximize our time both at the top of the towers and in downtown Manhattan.

He won the argument. The next day, instead of being in downtown Manhattan, we stood on Garret Mountain in Clifton, N.J. and watched the towers come down.

Like millions of Americans, I struggled with what I saw. I joined the thousands who enlisted in the military out of a sense of duty. I also felt an immense amount of hatred in my heart. I hated Osama Bin Laden, terrorists, people who made excuses for what happened, and those who thought we should not have plunged headfirst into what we called an expanding “War on Terror.” I told myself that going into Iraq (where I went as a Marine) was a mistake, but that the larger goal of fighting terrorism justified our expanding military operations around the world. And boy, did we expand the fight to include a litany of countries bombed and trillions of dollars spent.

But we accomplished our goals, right? Well, 25 years later, it has become apparent that we have not defeated terrorism. The world is a less safe place despite our actions, and Bin Laden achieved one of his main goals: to bleed America dry and force its economy to buckle.

Although he initially wanted the U.S. to withdraw its forces and influence from the Middle East, he realized rather quickly that the U.S. had made a huge blunder by expanding the war into Iraq. In 2004, he released a video that then sounded like a madman yelling nonsense on the street corner. The truth is, it hit very close to home then — we just didn’t want to admit it because of pride. As of 2026, the late terrorist’s rantings are now backed by facts and figures.

“ We are continuing this policy in bleeding America to the point of bankruptcy ” was a claim that Bin Laden made in his 2004 video. He likened the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq to the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan that lasted through the 1980s. He studied the U.S. and its actions in Vietnam trying to rely on military spending, body counts and struggling with insurgency groups. American politicians could not afford to look weak on terror, so they expanded operations all over the Middle East and the world.

And it wasn’t just one political party, either. Many Democrats railed against President Bush’s invasion of Iraq and the blunder of Bin Laden’s escape at Tora Bora, only to make excuses when President Obama decided that drone strikes were the new norm and that we needed to keep troops in Afghanistan after Bin Laden was killed in 2011.

In short, Bin Laden knew in 2004 that we would continue the war even after his body was dropped into the ocean’s abyss.

We saw Al Qaeda’s soldiers and other Islamists branch off and form other groups with their own intentions. The Islamic State grew out of the Al Qaeda in Iraq organization and quickly capitalized on the Syrian civil war. Iran took notes on U.S. actions and ramped up operations and spending involving Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis and Shiite militias in Iraq. We have seen Islamist cells strike in Kenya, Nigeria, India, France and dozens of other countries.

As these groups have grown, so has our spending to combat every real or perceived threat. In 2004, the national debt was $7 trillion dollars. Since 2001, military spending has added $8 trillion to our national debt which is now $40 trillion. Post 9/11 military spending is now at $18 trillion. And that doesn’t even include money we spend domestically. The Department of Homeland Security alone cost us $1.2 trillion. The interest on the borrowing is $1.1 trillion, more than twice the amount spent on all the Veterans Affairs medical and disability expenses that these wars have trebled.

We are now told that we need to spend $1.5 trillion annually to keep us safe. We are dangerously low on missiles because of the war with Iran. We are spending billions on military contractors who do not deliver the weapons to keep us safe . We fought and engaged in war games with Ukraine to see if we could handle modern warfare, and it turns out that we can’t . We are sending troops out over and over again to the point where they are breaking not just when they come home but while out on deployment .

Bin Laden once blasted Bush for his greed for oil and his corporate cronyism. After all, companies like Halliburton did well while our country did not. “The darkness of black gold (oil) blurred his vision and insight, and he gave priority to private interests over the public interests of America,” said Bin Laden .

You could use the same sentence now when it comes to Iran. At the conflict’s inception, we were spending millions of dollars to combat Iranian drones that cost thousands. This was something Bin Laden bragged about in 2004. “Every dollar of al Qaeda defeated a million [U.S.] dollars.”

Former CIA agent John Kiriakou recently claimed that if the U.S. stopped fighting wars, we would enter a recession . That is perhaps dramatic, but the ever-growing defense budget and national debt should make us wonder whether we are on the right course.

Should we wave the white flag when it comes to Islamic terror? Absolutely not. But we really need to take stock of the lives lost, trillions spent, and freedoms surrendered in the war on terror and realize that our actions are creating exactly what Bin Laden wanted.

As a veteran of Iraq who watched the Twin Towers fall with my own eyes, I think it is past time to go back to the drawing board on our war on terror. Because at this point, Bin Laden seems to have won.

Joslin Joseph is a recipient of the Military Reporters and Editors award for Best Commentary / Opinion. A graduate of Harvard and Ohio State, he is a Marine veteran who served in Iraq. He currently lives in Anaheim, Calif.

articles.title: Fetal personhood and the anti-freedom Republicans
articles.summary: The consequences of politicians defining a fertilized egg as a legal person deserving the full protection of the law are far-reaching.
articles.body:
I’m not sure how we got to the point where comedians are some of our best political commentators. Maybe a bit of dark humor makes it easier to keep paying attention when there’s so much bad news to digest.

John Oliver’s recent show exploring the concept of fetal personhood — and the horrifying consequences when that concept is put into law — demonstrated that he is one of the best of our comedians-turned-explainers.

Personhood advocates are the hard-core, no-compromises wing of the anti-abortion movement, insisting that fertilized eggs deserve full legal and constitutional rights from the moment of conception. A defining trait is their opposition to any exceptions for rape or incest in laws banning abortion.

Not long ago, these were considered fringe positions even within the pro-life movement. But anti-abortion extremism has increasingly become the norm among today’s Republican politicians — even though voters often reject it when given the chance. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has pushed legislation to enshrine in law his belief that life begins at conception.

And, as Oliver noted, once the Supreme Court’s MAGA majority overturned Roe v. Wade, all the guardrails have been eliminated . That has meant more women being brutalized by the legal system in states with abortion bans.

The consequences of politicians defining a fertilized egg as a legal person deserving the full protection of the law are far-reaching. In states that treat the rights of an embryo or fetus as predominant, pregnant women lose their agency as human beings. Instead, they are treated, in Oliver’s words, as “incubators” — or, in the words of an anti-abortion politician he quoted, “hosts.”

Women have suffered grievous harm, and some have died , because they were denied urgently needed lifesaving care because doctors and hospitals feared persecution by anti-abortion zealots if they carried out emergency abortions.

Oliver highlighted the case of a Wisconsin woman who had engaged in drug use but stopped once she realized she was pregnant; officials arrested her and put her in prison to “protect” the fetus she was carrying — as if the stress of being in jail and solitary confinement did not carry its own health risks.

Other women who lose pregnancies may have their grief compounded by criminal investigations into whether they may did something to cause a miscarriage. About one-quarter of pregnancies end in miscarriage, so that’s a lot of opportunities for intrusive government officials to traumatize women and their families needlessly.

These abuses of power make it clear that anti-abortion strategists were lying when they said for so many years that they were not interested in punishing women. It turns out that they are very interested in punishing women.

Princeton University Professor Robert George — one of the most prominent anti-abortion and anti-gay and transgender advocates in the country — filed an amicus brief in the Dobbs case challenging Roe v. Wade. He urged the Supreme Court to rule that “prenatal persons” are persons under the 14th Amendment from the moment of conception. States should be required to treat abortion as homicide, he argued, adding that Congress would have to enforce such a ruling “if states failed in their duties.”

Personhood laws also threaten to criminalize some common forms of birth control as well as in-vitro fertilization techniques that are widely used by couples facing fertility challenges. A 2024 Alabama Supreme Court ruling declared that a couple’s frozen embryos, which someone had allegedly negligently destroyed, must be treated as persons for purposes of a wrongful death lawsuit in state court.

The relentlessness of anti-abortion advocates and politicians has threatened other tools that empower women and families, like apps that track menstrual cycles. Once Roe v. Wade was overturned and Republican politicians started passing ever-more-draconian abortion bans, women have been rightly concerned about whether data from period-tracking apps could be misused by aggressive prosecutors.

In other words, the same movement that tells women their primary purpose is to have lots of babies is taking steps to make it harder for many women to have children.

That same disconnect was evident in the way some right-wing activists freaked out when Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) decided to speak with admirable openness about her decision to freeze some of her eggs, another step many women take to preserve the option of becoming parents.

It is undeniable that Republican politicians have become increasingly hostile to freedom, individual rights, and bodily autonomy, adopting Christian nationalists’ eagerness to use government power to impose their worldview on all of us.

We see it in the cruelty of Republicans’ aggressive attacks on transgender people. We see it in the religious-right’s energetic campaign to overturn marriage equality. And we see it in the expansive efforts to censor books and classroom materials and impose right-wing ideology on libraries and museums.

We also see it in the eagerness of Republican politicians like Ken Paxton to distort the truth and try to score political points , as he has by loudly inserting himself in a high-profile surrogacy dispute.

The last thing any American should want is some cynical politician like Paxton inserting himself into families’ most difficult moments and consequential decisions. It sounds like a sick joke, but it is all too commonplace — and deadly serious.

Svante Myrick is president of People For the American Way .

articles.title: Forget the recent socialist shift — Democrats are ready for an FDR revival
articles.summary: By 2028, most Americans will be ready to shift their attention to someone other than Trump. And the candidate who disavows the DSA and embraces the muscular, practical liberalism of FDR is the one who will likely prevail.
articles.body:
Appearing on “ Fox News Sunday ,” Megan Romer, co-chair of the Democratic Socialists of America, was asked and answered whether the DSA supports the following :

Abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement — check.

Abolishing U.S. borders and giving illegal aliens amnesty — check.

Eliminating public ownership of most large corporation — check.

Those affirmative answers were a gift to President Trump. Always ready to exploit any Democratic weakness, the president believes he has a winning strategy for 2026: “ All we have to do is define our opponent as being a communist or a socialist or somebody who is going to destroy our country .”

During the Cold War, Americans recoiled at the communist label. Sixty-four percent favored taking repressive measures against the U.S. Communist Party; 67 percent believed communists should be banned from holding civil service jobs; 77 percent said no person could be a “good Christian and at the same time be a member of the Communist Party.”

Taking note of the Republican attacks, Rep. Jim McGovern (D-Mass.) asks , “Did we accidentally step into a time machine?”

The Democratic Socialists of America is having a moment. Last year, Zohran Mamdani was elected mayor of New York City. He used his political clout to back another socialist congressional candidate, Darializa Avila Chevalier, who beat Rep. Adriano Espaillat (D-N.Y.) in their primary contest. In Colorado, Democrat Diana DeGette fell to socialist challenger Melat Kiros. In Michigan, Democratic Socialists of America member Donavan McKinney ousted incumbent Democrat Shri Thanedar . And in Florida, Angie Nixon, another member, shockingly won the Democratic nomination for the U.S. Senate despite being vastly outspent.

Other left-leaning Democrats have also posted significant wins. Abdul El-Sayed is the Democratic senatorial nominee in Michigan. Progressive activist William Lawrence beat two moderate Democrats in a congressional primary.

But the defeat of Democratic Socialists member Francesca Hong in the Wisconsin gubernatorial primary proves that even if Democrats are angry, they are not entirely stupid. Canceling Thanksgiving and abolishing the police are deal-breakers.

Democrats realize our democracy is at stake. And pragmatic Democrats want their party to win.

A New York Times/Siena College poll shows 52 percent of Democrats want their party to move to the center. And 50 percent and 46 percent, respectively, favor centrist positions on crime and immigration — two issues Republicans like to call their own.

Listen to Patricia Soto, a Democrat from Pinecrest, Fla. On immigration, she says , “The Democrats need to underscore that this is a nation of laws and regulations that are fair,” while adding, “We do need to address the immigrants that are already here without vindictiveness, without making them all the bad guys, because that’s not true.”

The fact that most Democrats want to occupy the center, however, does not mean they oppose major changes in government. Democrats want an activist government — especially when it comes to insuring health care, providing child care, overhauling the tax system, making millionaires and billionaires pay their fair share, and shoring up Social Security and Medicare.

Advocating a muscular liberalism is not the same as supporting the socialist agenda. Democrats would be wise to remember the words of President Franklin Roosevelt, who told voters in 1932: “The country demands bold, persistent experimentation. It is common sense to take a method and try it. If it fails, admit it frankly and try another. But above all, try something.”

Democrats want their next president to emulate Roosevelt’s approach and focus on them. And the party has taken steps to ensure that their 2028 nominee can win, by rebalancing its nomination calendar. The Democratic National Committee has authorized six states to be the first to cast ballots in the 2028 primary season: South Carolina on Jan. 22; Nevada on Feb. 1; New Hampshire on Feb. 8; New Mexico on Feb. 15; Michigan on Feb. 22; and Virginia on Feb. 29.

Democratic consultant John W. McCarthy notes that in these early primary voting states, there are 4.6 million Blacks; 4.2 million Latinos; 1.4 million Asian Americans, Native Hawaiians, and Pacific Islanders; 370,000 Native Americans; 14 million non-college voters; 2.8 million young adults between the ages of 18 and 24; 1.1 union workers; and 2.1 million military veterans and military voters.

Former DNC chair Jamie Harrison has some sage advice for any would-be socialist candidate: “If you hate the Democratic Party, then please don’t run for our nomination. Don’t use our resources. Don’t rely on our volunteers. Don’t use our infrastructure.”

Harrison’s warning is apt but unnecessary. By 2028, most Americans will be ready to shift their attention to someone other than Trump. And the candidate who disavows the Democratic Socialists of America organization and embraces Roosevelt’s muscular, practical liberalism is the one who will likely prevail.

By rebalancing their party, Democrats can once again reclaim the title Franklin D. Roosevelt used for it: “ The Democracy .”

John Kenneth White is a professor emeritus at the Catholic University of America who writes on Substack . His latest book, coauthored with Matthew R. Kerbel, is titled “ Democracy on the Edge: The Trump Elections and the Future of American Politics.”

articles.body:
Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) said Sunday he is “very confident” in Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) winning her GOP primary runoff for Senate in the Palmetto State this week.

During an appearance Sunday on “Meet the Press,” NBC News’s Kristen Welker pressed Scott on his level of confidence in Graham’s victory in the runoff, to which he said he was “very confident.”

“It’s one of the reasons why I waited 30 days to make sure that I felt like she was ready,” he said. “I can tell you, as the senior senator, for the great state of South Carolina, the person I want in the Senate with me, Darline Graham, representing the people of South Carolina. Easy choice.”

Earlier this month , the race to fill the seat on the November ballot went to a primary runoff, which occurs Tuesday, with Graham and Rep. Ralph Norman (R) battling it out for the GOP nomination.

Scott also said “there’s no doubt” Graham is qualified to be a senator despite a recent debate slip-up on an answer about national security.

“One other thing that’s really important: I watched her on the campaign trail. I watched her go through two funerals for her brother, and then I watched her carefully for 30 days in the Senate, casting deciding votes for the AG [attorney general], working on getting her first bill passed, the Russia sanctions bill. What did I assess? Highly qualified, incredibly competent, ready for primetime,” Scott said.

Last week, President Trump defended Graham after she said in a South Carolina GOP Senate primary debate that she was “not that informed on national security” but backed “the military.” The senator had been asked if Taiwan and the South China Sea are American national security issues.

“She’s very smart, and she was being honest. She’s into the price of groceries. … She is going to do what the military wants, and really what the president wants,” Trump said Friday before leaving for South Carolina to rally with Graham in Myrtle Beach.

Trump has endorsed Graham since she was appointed to finish her late brother’s, Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), term.

articles.title: Trump boasts his endorsements are ‘stronger than ever’
articles.summary: President Trump on Sunday boasted his endorsements are “stronger than ever,” despite some prominent losses in recent primaries. “My Endorsements are stronger than ever — Not to mention the fact that good people are getting elected that never had the chance,” the president wrote in a Sunday evening Truth Social post, boasting that 254 candidates…
articles.body:
President Trump on Sunday boasted his endorsements are “stronger than ever,” despite some prominent losses in recent primaries.

“My Endorsements are stronger than ever — Not to mention the fact that good people are getting elected that never had the chance,” the president wrote in a Sunday evening Truth Social post , boasting that 254 candidates with his backing won their races this cycle.

According to a graphic included with the post, that translates to a 97 percent overall success rate in 262 races.

However, Trump-endorsed candidates lost congressional races in Florida, Tennessee and Michigan in recent weeks.

Rep. Cory Mills (R-Fla.) lost his reelection bid to TV anchor Ryan Elijah, while Rep. Andy Ogles (R-Tenn.) lost his reelection bid to former Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher.

Amir Hassan in Michigan also fell short in his run for a House seat after receiving Trump’s endorsement.

Trump’s endorsements will be put to the test again this week, with Trump-backed Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) facing Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) in a runoff for a Senate seat in the Palmetto State. The president’s pick for Oklahoma governor, Mike Mazzei, is also vying against state Attorney General Gentner Drummond (R) for the party’s nomination.

The president on Sunday said that those who lost their races with his endorsement were already “impossible” candidates.

“It is an Honor that I take very seriously,” Trump said of his endorsements. “The few that lost were done out of loyalty. It was almost impossible for them to win but, I felt obligated to go with them because they were, in my opinion, good people.”

articles.title: Dethroned Miss North Carolina USA files lawsuit, says she was stripped of crown over conservative beliefs
articles.summary: Brittany Boltinhouse claims that pageant organizers conspired to replace and defame her over her support for President Trump, among other conservative figures.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Brittany Boltinhouse, who was recently dethroned as Miss North Carolina USA , has filed a lawsuit against the organizers of the Miss USA and Miss North Carolina USA pageants, claiming she was targeted for her “conservative Christian” views.

Boltinhouse was stripped of her title earlier this month over “recently surfaced information” that went against the “standards and values” of the pageant, a statement released by A Blaize Productions, the organizers of Miss North Carolina USA, announced on Aug. 5. At the time, A Blaize Productions did not detail any of the “information” that led to their decision. But in a separate statement, Miss USA president and CEO Thom Brodeur appeared to indicate incidents of discriminatory actions or statements.

“The Miss USA organization does not tolerate racism, homophobia, transphobia nor language that strips any person of their dignity — whoever they are,” Brodeur’s statement, made public on Instagram on Aug. 6, read.

Reports later surfaced of Boltinhouse using the word “n—a” on social media in 2017 and 2019.

In the lawsuit, which names the Miss USA organization and A Blaize Productions among the defendants, lawyers for Boltinhouse did not deny that their client used this term on social media. But they contended that the posts are “in no way evidence she is a racist, homophobe, transphobe or a bigot who should be shunned from public life as Defendants set about and conspired to cause with their defamatory social media posts.”

Instead, Boltinhouse’s lawsuit argues that pageant organizers conspired to replace Boltinhouse and defame her over her support for conservative politicians and figures, including President Donald Trump, Andrew and Tristan Tate, and Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk. Another social media post included in the documents shows Boltinhouse had spoken out against President Joe Biden’s “Transgender Day of Visibility” in 2024, suggesting it was part of a “moral decay” that went against American and Christian values.

Boltinhouse, as part of a TPUSA trip, also attended Trump’s speech on the Ellipse on Jan. 6, 2021, the lawsuit says, though she did not “approach or enter the Capitol Building” afterward, according to court documents obtained by Nexstar.

“Defendants hid from the public the real reason they dethroned Brittany: [S]he is a conservative Christian,” her lawyers claim in the lawsuit.

They further allege that an apology from Boltinhouse, which was mentioned in Brodeur’s Aug. 6 statement, had never been approved or agreed to by their client.

Boltinhouse is seeking compensatory and punitive damages, as well as attorneys’ fees.

Representatives for the Miss USA organization or A Blaize Productions did not immediately return a request for comment.

Boltinhouse, from Duplin County, North Carolina, won the Miss North Carolina USA pageant on June 28, 2026. Speaking with The Duplin Times after her win, she said she entered the pageant — her first ever — to get in touch with her femininity after starting a flooring business with her husband.

“I’m in such a male-dominated field that it didn’t allow me to be girly,” she told the outlet.

Boltinhouse, who was 27 when she won the crown, was slated to compete in the upcoming Miss USA pageant, which kicks off this week in Miami. North Carolina is instead being represented by Myla Hadley, who was crowned in Boltinhouse’s stead.

“I understand the seriousness and level of prestige that this title carries, and I can confidently say that both my team and I are ready to take this on,” Hadley wrote earlier this month on Instagram.

articles.title: Existing White House bunker undermines need for East Wing renovation, officials reportedly say
articles.summary: A new report says the White House already has an existing underground bunker for the president and his staff in case of national security threats, potentially undercutting administration claims of an urgent need for the East Wing renovations. Three former officials told The Washington Post that the White House complex currently includes a subterranean, highly…
articles.body:
A new report says the White House already has an existing underground bunker for the president and his staff in case of national security threats, potentially undercutting administration claims of an urgent need for the East Wing renovations.

Three former officials told The Washington Post that the White House complex currently includes a subterranean, highly secure facility of the kind President Trump has said is needed under his proposed ballroom. Two of the officials reportedly said the bunker can withstand a nuclear blast and is capable of housing the president and dozens of staffers for weeks on end.

The officials say the military complex undercuts the need for the current East Wing renovations, which the Trump administration has argued are needed to mitigate threats to the president and those who tail him on a daily basis.

The facility sits 60 feet underground and was completed during the Obama administration, as reported by The Washington Post.

Under former President Franklin D. Roosevelt, an underground bunker now known as the Presidential Emergency Operations Center was installed below the White House’s East Wing complex to deal with potential threats tied to World War II.

During that time, there was also a secret tunnel developed , so the president could be taken to the Treasury Department building, adjacent to the White House in the need for a swift exit from the White House campus.

“Recent events such as the foiled attack on the historic UFC Freedom 250 event at the White House proves exactly why the East Wing Modernization Project is severely needed for large scale events, which include drone proof structures and drone ports among other critical security enhancements,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told The Hill.

The Trump administration argues the former East Wing offered no suitable options for modern day threats.

“As declarations explain, the old East Wing’s structure could not bear the weight of necessary security materials—e.g., bullet- and blast-proof windows, fortified walls and roofing, missile-resistant columns, and protective partitioning,” attorneys for the federal government wrote in court filings .

“The military installation underground also required massive changes—e.g., a military-grade ventilation system, revamped hospital, and medical facilities—that could not be built with a fragile structure on top. Those security needs inform what any such above-ground structure must entail,” they added.

The National Trust for Historic Preservation, a nonprofit chartered by Congress to protect places of national significance, has filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration alleging the president did not have the authority to unilaterally overhaul the White House campus.

As a result, federal appeals and district judges previously issued blocks to the administration’s above-ground construction on the ballroom, ruling the project needs congressional authorization.

On Friday, Chief Justice John Roberts temporarily blocked a ruling that was set to halt construction, ruling that work can briefly continue as the Supreme Court weighs Trump’s emergency plea for it to get involved.

The Trump administration argues the project above and below ground are one in the same.

“The government has never suggested the below-ground bunker and above-ground ballroom were independent. To the contrary, as construction and plans proceeded, the government explained the interconnectedness and diminishing flexibility for changes,” attorneys for the federal government wrote in an opening brief .

articles.title: Knowledge is power: Why America needs economic security intelligence
articles.summary: To counter economic coercion from China and other authoritarian states, the authors propose that the State Department establish annual Economic Security Intelligence Reports to help the United States identify and mitigate systemic economic risks.
articles.body:
America was unprepared for its trade war with China, but it shouldn’t have been. As Beijing cut off access to critical minerals, the United States had no response but a quiet retreat. The Trump administration’s recent push to rebuild mining and processing capacity is welcome, but it comes more than a decade late. Strategic surprises of this kind are avoidable—but only if the United States systematically monitors economic security risks before they become crises. A new system of country-level Economic Security Intelligence Reports should become a cornerstone of American economic statecraft .

In 2010, China put the world on notice, weaponizing supply chains by cutting off rare earth exports to Japan during a territorial dispute. For 15 years, Washington stood idle as China deepened its dominance across critical minerals, batteries, shipping and industrial inputs essential to American manufacturing. Today, China produces 98 percent of the eight heavy rare earth elements, and once again is restricting access for both Japan and the United States.

Beijing is making the most of its economic leverage to weaken American competitors, imposing additional rare earth restrictions on key U.S. customers just this June. The International Energy Agency now estimates that full implementation of China’s rare earth export controls could put an annual $6.5 trillion in downstream production at risk—7 percent of global GDP excluding China.

The surprise is not China’s behavior but America’s failure to anticipate it. A key constraint is Washington’s lack of a systematic framework for identifying and monitoring emerging economic security risks. That gap is increasingly untenable.

China’s mineral monopolies were not the inevitable product of superior geology — China dominates the market for processed cobalt, copper and lithium even though it is dependent on imports for the raw form of those minerals. Instead, Beijing has built dominance through state intervention: massive subsidies, chronic overcapacity, price manipulation, and lax labor and environmental standards — letting unprofitable firms undercut and drive out Western competitors. These practices also discourage the long-term investment needed to develop alternatives, making diversification economically irrational even when it is strategically essential.

Western firms cannot indefinitely sustain losses in pursuit of geopolitical influence. With Beijing’s finger on the scale, Chinese companies can — and often do.

Subsidies create monopolies, monopolies provide leverage, leverage enables coercion, and coercion reinforces monopolies. This self-sustaining cycle is swallowing an increasing share of global manufacturing, with China on pace to account for 45 percent of the world’s industrial production by 2030.

China’s predation is only one manifestation of a broader challenge posed by authoritarian economics — from Iran’s chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz to Russia’s weaponization of European gas dependence. If the United States intends to place economic security at the center of trade policy, it cannot keep treating fundamentally different economic systems as though they play by the same rules.

What is needed is what we have called a “ Near-Global Economy ”: a framework that deepens integration among trusted market economies while reducing dependence on state-driven competitors.

Any such response to authoritarian economics, however, will require a new form of intelligence — the rigorous and comprehensive assessment of the economic security posture of allies, partners, rivals and rogues.

For U.S. policymakers to assess the risks posed by America’s major trading partners, the executive branch needs the capacity to systematically collect and analyze this information. One solution: an annual, country-by-country Economic Security Intelligence Report created by the State Department — leveraging America’s diplomatic missions to map each nation’s economic security vulnerability, opportunity and strategic reliability.

The value of such a report would not lie in compiling statistics but in answering practical questions: Which partners are quietly serving as pass-throughs for adversary capital? Which possess strong legal authorities but weak enforcement? Which are becoming more trustworthy over time and which less so?

Reliable partners should demonstrate commitment to market-oriented policies, protect intellectual property, limit market-distorting subsidies, and enforce baseline labor, environmental, and antitrust standards. Washington should also evaluate whether partners have the legal authorities, institutional capacity, and political will to support U.S. sanctions, export controls, and anti-money-laundering laws. Partners should meet baseline standards for beneficial ownership registries and investment screening mechanisms. Partners need to prevent transshipment and enforce rules of origin .

The goal is not more reports or more bureaucrats — it is actionable intelligence to inform trade, investment and national security policy. Its findings could justify corrective tariffs, guide financing by the Development Finance Corporation and Export-Import Bank, and set prerequisites for defense-industrial cooperation and trusted technology initiatives. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s reorganization of the State Department has placed economic statecraft at the center of American diplomacy; the Economic Security Intelligence Report would give this effort an operational backbone.

The United States should not only grade others — it should apply the same framework to itself. Anonymous shell companies, trusts and opaque legal structures let hostile actors disguise themselves as American businesses, undermining sanctions, anti-money laundering efforts, and ultimately, national security. Applying honest standards at home would strengthen both the report’s credibility and America’s own resilience.

The United States would never enter a military alliance without understanding its allies’ capabilities and vulnerabilities. It should be no less careful building the economic alliances that will define the next international order. Strategic surprise in the economic domain is not inevitable, but avoiding it requires treating economic intelligence as a core instrument of national power. To avoid strategic surprise tomorrow, America must monitor economic security risks today.

Josh Birenbaum is the deputy director of the Center on Economic and Financial Power (CEFP) at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. Antonia-Laura Pup is a PhD researcher at the European University Institute and former CEFP intern.

articles.title: Mamdani jumps into Democratic Party feud, alleging boss seeking to subvert 'will of voters'
articles.summary: Zohran Mamdani opposes Rodneyse Bichotte Hermelyn's push to add voting members to the Brooklyn Democratic Party executive committee before a fall vote.
articles.body:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is opposing a last-minute push to overhaul Brooklyn Democratic Party rules, arguing the proposed changes would undermine voters after reformers made gains in the June primary.

"I very much oppose these proposed changes, by the current Brooklyn Democratic Party chair," Mamdani said. "I oppose them because they are an attempt to circumnavigate the will of voters."

The proposals from Brooklyn Democratic Party chair Rodneyse Bichotte Hermelyn would add more than two dozen voting members to the party's executive committee, which will choose the party chair this fall, after a slate of reformers won 22 district leader seats in the June primary, according to the City Reporter .

Nyc Taxpayers Could Pay Twice Under Mamdani's City-owned Grocery Store Plan

The newly elected district leaders will not take their seats until the fall, and Bichotte Hermelyn and her supporters still hold a majority as current district leaders prepare to vote on the proposed changes Tuesday night, according to the outlet.

Bichotte Hermelyn has described the changes as an effort to broaden participation in the party .

"We want to create a perception of inclusiveness," she told NY1 . In a video released by the Brooklyn Democratic organization, she said the proposals would "expand leadership" and "expand representation."

The reformers have backed longtime Sunset Park district leader Julio Peña to become the next party chair. If the proposed changes pass, the additional voting members would take part in the fall leadership election.

Vice President Jd Vance Blasts Mamdani, El-sayed, Aoc And Ossoff In Rapid-fire Tiktok Roast

Mamdani said the Brooklyn Democratic Party should reflect what New Yorkers want, rather than the kind of politics that has left people "disengaged and disaffected with politics at large."

New York Attorney General Letitia James and Public Advocate Jumaane Williams have also urged the party not to move forward with the changes.

"New Yorkers deserve leaders who are committed to serving their communities, not rewriting rules to hold onto power," they said in a joint statement obtained by City and State New York. "Changing the makeup of an executive committee on the eve of a leadership vote goes against what we believe in as Democrats and should not move forward."

Another proposal would give former party chairs a vote in future leadership elections even after they are no longer district leaders .

According to the City Reporter, that appears to mean former party chair Clarence Norman could vote on future party leadership. Norman resigned in 2005 after multiple corruption convictions, including one for soliciting bribes from judicial nominees.

After the leadership election, another proposed change would allow additional voting members to be appointed from each Assembly district, potentially bringing the executive committee to about 90 members.

articles.title: Trump’s Taiwan two-step
articles.summary: South Korea is not a happy country. It was unwilling to help President Trump’s team keep the Strait of Hormuz open. So the petulant president decided it was time to rekindle his love affair with North Korea’s dictator, Kim Jung Un, and punish the South by cutting short joint exercises. One wonders if the logical consequence will…
articles.body:
South Korea is not a happy country. It was unwilling to help President Trump’s team keep the Strait of Hormuz open. So the petulant president decided it was time to rekindle his love affair with North Korea’s dictator, Kim Jung Un, and punish the South by cutting short joint exercises.

One wonders if the logical consequence will be the South’s acquisition of nuclear weapons, as it can no longer trust the Trump administration to honor its defense commitments to Seoul.

What happens when China’s President Xi Jingping meets with President Trump next month? Suppose a Trump Taiwan two-step tango takes place and Trump decides there is no reason for the U.S. to go to war or to defend Taiwan, should China invade.

Trump’s argument, before his ill-advised war with Iran, could have been that about two thirds of Americans would not support going to war over Taiwan. But after the bungled Iran “excursion,” opposition to a war with China must surely be greater.

Taiwan’s internal politics reinforces that preference. Taiwan has the resources to create a “ Porcupine Defense ” that would make any Chinese invasion very costly and thus unlikely. But it has not done so. Taiwan still depends on the U.S. for its ultimate defense.

Of the 113 seats in the Yuan , Taiwan’s Parliament, 52 are held by the Kuomintang party, which supports some form of reconciliation with the mainland; 51 are held Democratic People’s Party, whch wishes to remain separate; and there are 10 other seats. That is one reason why a full Porcupine Defense has not been implemented.

China probably is taking the long view — that at some stage, Taiwan will chose to be absorbed.

Trump could expedite that process, working out a deal with Xi, just as he may negotiate a modus operandi with Kim. In that case, the U.S. would not be prepared or required to defend Taiwan if Xi makes a promise or commitment not to invade. Perhaps he would even help to resolve the war with Iran, greatly easing demands on the U.S. military.

The U.S. National Defense Strategy sets as a top priority to deter China in the Indo-Pacific through strength, not confrontation, to prevent access to the first island chain. The strategic reality is that China has set up a powerful perimeter to prevent its being denied access . With its longest range missiles and aviation units, its weapons engagement zone extends more than 1,500 miles from China’s borders.

In unclassified war games, this zone holds any surface forces at sea and ashore at substantial risk, meaning that high casualties are quite possible in any conflict.

But the U.S. has a better alternative. For much of the Cold War, it maintained the ability to wage war to defend NATO at the conventional and nuclear levels, for which it maintained substantial tactical or battlefield nuclear weapons and strategic forces through it bomber, ballistic submarine and land-based missiles.

Trump could state, as his insurance policy, that the U.S. has both conventional and nuclear forces ready to make any invasion of Taiwan a disaster. Although the analogy with NATO lacks the Article Five commitment — that “an attack against one shall be considered an attack against all” — such a threat should suffice to keep China from making a big mistake.

From Trump’s perspective, this would be a trifecta. Whether North Korea and China would be helpful in allowing him to extricate himself from Iran, that could occur. While this approach may not alter the war in Ukraine, it would permit Trump to defuse potential tensions in Korea, alter the commitment to Taiwan and improve U.S.-China relations.

It would not be so bad if Trump could execute this Taiwan two step tango. But I would not bet the future on an administration with such a poor record of execution.

Harlan Ullman is senior adviser at Washington’s Atlantic Council, chairman of a private company, and principal author of the doctrine of shock and awe. His next book, co-written with Field Marshal The Lord David Richards, former UK chief of defense and due out this Fall, is “Who Thinks Best Wins: How Decisive Strategic Thinking Will Prevent Global Chaos. “

articles.title: New York supermarkets sue over Mamdani’s municipal grocery stores
articles.summary: A group of grocers in New York City filed two separate lawsuits on Monday against Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration following the proposal of municipal grocery stores across the Big Apple. Plaintiffs united under the Multicultural Business Coalition sued Mamdani in state court, alleging their civil rights will be violated if city-run grocery stores are opened. …
articles.body:
A group of grocers in New York City filed two separate lawsuits on Monday against Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration following the proposal of municipal grocery stores across the Big Apple.

Plaintiffs united under the Multicultural Business Coalition sued Mamdani in state court, alleging their civil rights will be violated if city-run grocery stores are opened.

The second lawsuit alleges Mamdani’s administration didn’t engage in a proper analysis of the impact municipal grocery stores with reduced prices will have on current grocers.

“Plaintiffs have been denied equal protection where the Plaintiffs, predominately immigrant and minority owned grocery stores, are unable to offer similarly discounted products of the NYC-GP, and therefore, the former are being unduly denied the equal protection of the subsidized municipal grocery stores (i.e., NYC-GP), where the Defendants have failed to take corrective action, namely meaningfully study and analysis to avoid furthering historic discriminatory exclusion, and exclusion generally,” the first lawsuit , obtained by Fox Business Network, states.

“Therefore, the Plaintiffs are suffering undue harm,” attorneys for the plaintiffs add.

Grocers, represented by Mark Jaffe, the president of the Greater New York Chamber of Commerce, said the municipal stores offered to “sell food items 30 percent below the market-rate, a rate that rivals or exceeds Walmart discounts,” the second filing obtained by the New York Post states.

For years, grocers within the boundaries of New York City have fought to keep large retailers like Walmart outside the city’s market, afraid an “untold amount of opportunity for minority businesses and small business at large” would be eliminated, the lawsuit states.

Plaintiffs argue the five planned city-run grocery stores set to open next year with $70 million supported by taxpayers would have the same chilling effect.

Once a month the municipal grocery stores will evaluate prices and set the cost for food at 30 percent below retailers.

Mamdani has said he believes the measure will help crush inflation, cut overhead costs and stabilize prices across the city while giving residents more affordable grocery options.

The city will own the land and cover overhead costs like rent and construction while a private operator, selected through a request for proposals, will manage daily operations under a contract, according to Mamdani’s office.

“We are talking about a reflection of a cost-of-living crisis that has seen grocery prices increase by about 30 percent over the last few years, and we’re also talking about delivering five city-run grocery stores in a city of 8.5 million people that has more than a thousand grocery stores,” Mamdani said Monday at a press conference.

“And we’ve seen, in fact, with Essex Street Market in Manhattan, as well as Moore Street Market in Brooklyn, a model where the city has subsidized groceries and it has not had a negative effect on bodegas around them or on grocery stores around them,” he added.

His office and Jaffe did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

It’s Monday. We might technically still have about a month left of summer, but it’s feeling a bit like fall here in the D.C. area — just in time for the triumphant return tomorrow of the🧋Starbucks Pumpkin Spice Latte.

Awaiting details on “economic D-Day” for Iran

Runoffs on deck in South Carolina, Georgia

Measles outbreak collides with new school year

Programming note: Hello! We are Elliott Davis and Steff Danielle Thomas filling in for Cate. Please send your tips, comments and story ideas to edavis@thehill.com or sthomas@thehill.com .

The Associated Press | Mark Schiefelbein

The day President Trump first teased last week has arrived: The administration is set to unveil details about its economic offensive against Iran, which Trump and his allies have referred to as “economic D-Day.”

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent at 1 p.m. EDT is scheduled to announce sanctions against Iran and any country, business or banking institution supporting it. Bessent in a Sunday night social media post described the to-be-announced moves as marking the “single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled against an adversary.”

How has Tehran responded?: A top Iranian official over the weekend warned the country’s Middle East neighbors against joining the U.S.’s “economic war.” Iranian Supreme National Security Council leader Mohsen Rezaei also told state media that if Trump “wants to do something, we will retaliate in a seismic manner,” according to The Associated Press .

In advance of the operation, Iran’s rial currency dipped to a record-low 2.02 million to the U.S. dollar early Monday morning, the AP also reported .

Where does China come into this?: Because China is Iran’s largest trading partner and primary purchaser of its oil exports, the Trump administration’s “economic D-Day” offensive will also put Beijing in the crosshairs, The Hill’s Laura Kelly reports .

After Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced tariffs in response to the U.S.-imposed 50 percent duties that went into effect at 12:01 a.m. Saturday, Trump took aim at Canada in several Truth Social posts.

The president on Monday morning threatened to hit imported Canadian cars, trucks, auto parts and steel with new 50 percent tariffs that would go into effect on Jan. 1. (Happy New Year, Canada?)

The news came after Trump on Sunday claimed that Canada desires the “benefits of being a state, without being one,” in a reference to his previous talk of wanting to make the U.S.’s northern neighbor the 51st state.

Some pushback at home: A few notable Republicans have criticized the Trump administration’s moves. Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) over the weekend urged the White House to “consider the negative impact” the tariffs would have on Americans, while former Vice President Mike Pence said on Sunday that the “last thing we need” is a trade war with Canada.

The midterms are kicking into a higher gear this week, with lawmakers fanning out for fundraisers and campaign stops — and two big runoffs on deck Tuesday.

South Carolina gets top billing, where Sen. Darline Graham and Rep. Ralph Norman are duking it out for the GOP Senate nod. Trump gave Graham a final-week boost on Friday, hitting the trail for her in Myrtle Beach as she looks to turn her temporary appointment into a six-year job.

Georgia keeps the runoff theme going: Democratic candidate Marcye Scott is hoping to keep the House seat of her late father, former Rep. David Scott (D-Ga.), in the family. But first, she’ll have to get past former Gwinnett County Board of Education Chair Everton Blair Jr . in Tuesday’s all-Democratic faceoff.

Beyond the ballot: The campaign trail is only getting busier as August recess wraps up. Lawmakers are spending the week back home shaking hands, raising cash and making their case to voters, while party leaders are increasingly jumping into the races they think could tip control of Congress.

The calendar is quickly shrinking, too: Labor Day is just around the corner, marking the unofficial start of the fall sprint — and leaving candidates with little time to make their pitch before voters have the final say in November.

Iowa’s surprisingly tight Senate race is putting another statewide fight front and center: cancer. The Hawkeye State has the second-highest rate in the country.

Democrat state Rep. Josh Turek and Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson are making the issue part of their pitches as they battle to replace retiring Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa).

With the contest tightening, how each candidate tackles the state’s cancer crisis could prove to be a major X factor. The Hill’s Helen Huiskes explains more here .

Republicans and Democrats have found some rare common ground heading into the fall: Both think the other side is “radical.”

The label is quickly becoming a favorite midterm weapon, with Republicans tying the left to the Democratic Socialists of America, while Democrats are using it against Trump and his MAGA base.

In Florida, GOP gubernatorial candidate Rep. Byron Donalds is calling Democrat David Jolly “radically liberal,” while the label is also flying in Sen. Jon Ossoff ’s (D-Ga.) reelection fight.

📖 The Hill’s Amie Parnes lays it all out .

Alaska’s Senate race has a Dan Sullivan problem — there are three of them , and two are now weighing in on the ballot.

Former Anchorage Mayor Dan A. Sullivan is backing incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) over challenger Dan J. Sullivan , whom Republicans accuse of trying to confuse voters.

Students are heading back to class with an unwanted classmate: measles. The U.S. is closing in on 3,000 cases this year — a 35-year high — and health officials expect crowded classrooms to only add to the spread.

The timing isn’t great. Nonmedical vaccine exemptions among kindergartners hit a record 4.2 percent last school year, with 24 states reporting rates above 5 percent. 👓 Insiders can read more from The Hill’s Joseph Choi .

Enter the MMR debate: President Trump wants the three-in-one measles, mumps and rubella vaccine split into separate shots . Medical groups and others say there’s no scientific reason for the change — and warn it could turn two doses into as many as six doctor visits.

That could mean more copays, more scheduling headaches and more chances for kids to miss a dose. And it comes as officials, including Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz, have endorsed the measles vaccine amid the surge.

The tension: The administration is urging Americans to get vaccinated while simultaneously pushing to make the vaccination process more complicated.

articles.title: Trump wants cheaper beef. Republicans in key races warn his plan goes too far
articles.summary: Senate Republicans, including Tom Cotton and Tim Sheehy, push back on Trump's plan to import 300,000 metric tons of foreign ground beef to lower prices.
articles.body:
Senate Republicans racing to keep their grip on power have beef with President Donald Trump's latest affordability push.

A handful of Republicans in the upper chamber aren't happy with Trump's directive to allow hundreds of thousands of tons of foreign beef into the U.S. in a bid to lower grocery bills. It comes as Americans' struggles with everyday affordability have erupted as a key issue for voters across the country.

Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., who is up for re-election this cycle and is one of Trump's top allies in the Senate, argued that beef prices are high "for a simple reason: Our cattle herd is too small."

Trump Urged To Stop Targeting Fellow Republicans As Gop Fights To Keep Majority

"Imported beef below market prices will only put more pressure on our cattlemen," Cotton said on X. "I have advised the President against this ill-advised action in the past and I now urge him to reconsider. We need to support our cattlemen, grow the herd, and let the market work."

Trump last week announced on Truth Social his intent to flood the market with 300,000 metric tons of imported ground beef with a commitment that the product would be sold at 25% below current market prices over a 90-day span.

It comes as ground beef prices have soared to roughly $7 per pound, while the nation's cattle herd earlier this year hit historic lows not seen since the 1950s, according to data from the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA).

Top Gop Group Pumps $37M Into Fight On Key Issue Dominating Midterm Races: 'Much More To Come'

Trump defended his import plan as he headed to South Carolina to stump for Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., arguing "that's what the people want."

"That's what the voters want, and that's what I want. The ranchers are great. They're my people. I love the ranchers," Trump said. "They've done a fantastic job, but they admit that we need a little help in order to get the prices down, so that's what we're doing."

Neither Trump, nor the administration, has so far said which countries the ground beef would come from. But earlier this year, he signed an executive order similarly aimed at lowering beef prices by allowing an influx of 80,000 metric tons of beef trimmings from Argentina.

Republicans at the time privately fumed over the directive in a closed-door meeting in the Senate with Vice President JD Vance.

And now, Republicans running for office in America's heartland again disagree.

"I want to lower prices, but this is a bad idea," Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, said on X.

Senate Map Tightens As Top Forecaster Moves 3 Races Toward Democrats

Hinson is running in one of the tightest races in the country to replace retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa. Cook Political Report rated the race a toss-up last week.

Other in-cycle incumbents aren't thrilled with Trump's push, either. Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., charged, "This Hurts!," while Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., contended that he appreciated the work to "lower grocery prices," but warned that "short-term policy shifts do not equal long-term solutions."

"Flooding the market with lower quality beef compromises Nebraska farmers and ranchers," Ricketts said.

Trump's other key Senate allies aren't thrilled with the plan either.

Sen. Tim Sheehy, R-Mont., said he's advised Trump not to do this for the last year because it would harm American ranchers, "most of whom are MAGA Republicans."

"The president's heart is in the right place on wanting lower prices for the American people, and beef prices have been impacted by the Mexican screwworm ," Sheehy said. The White House and the USDA did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
